segments.narration: In 1883, a single sound ruptured eardrums forty miles away. Sailors nearby watched air pressure spike until barometers shattered.
Four hours later, people three thousand miles away heard artillery. Across the Indian Ocean, coastlines shook from an invisible blast.
Then, barometers in London and San Francisco began spiking hours apart. How could one sound hit every continent over and over?
It was the eruption of Krakatoa, exploding with two hundred megatons of force. The blast hurled a massive pressure wave through the atmosphere.
The pressure wave circled the Earth three and a half times.

verdicts.claim: In 1883, an explosion off the coast of Sumatra produced a sound that ruptured sailors' eardrums forty miles away.
verdicts.note: The article states that the sound ruptured the eardrums of sailors on a ship roughly 64 km (40 mi) away off Sumatra.

verdicts.claim: People living three thousand miles away in the Indian Ocean heard the sound four hours after the explosion.
verdicts.note: The article mentions people on islands in the western Indian Ocean approximately 3,000 miles away heard the sound nearly four hours after the eruption.

verdicts.claim: Barometers in London and San Francisco recorded recurring air pressure spikes hours apart from the blast wave.
verdicts.note: The article states that barographs worldwide recorded the wave multiple times, but it does not specifically mention London or San Francisco.

verdicts.claim: The 1883 Krakatoa eruption released energy equivalent to approximately two hundred megatons of TNT.
verdicts.note: The article explicitly estimates the energy released to be equal to about 200 megatonnes of TNT.

verdicts.claim: The atmospheric pressure wave from Krakatoa's eruption circled the Earth four times before dissipating.
verdicts.note: The article specifies that the pressure wave rounded the globe three and a half times (recorded seven times: four travelling away to its antipodal point and three travelling back).
verdicts.correction: The pressure wave circled the Earth three and a half times.
